title: Does a moon of Saturn have the ingredients for life?
blurb: Saturn's small moon Enceladus sprays water from a hidden ocean. Scientists found phosphorus, a key ingredient for life, in that spray.

cover.alt: The curved edge of Saturn's moon Enceladus in darkness, with bright jets of icy spray shooting up into space.

source.name: NASA
source.title: NASA Cassini Data Reveals Building Block for Life in Enceladus' Ocean

original.title: Detection of phosphates originating from Enceladus's ocean
original.authors: Frank Postberg, Yasuhito Sekine, Fabian Klenner, Christopher R. Glein and others

cards.b: Enceladus is a small, icy moon of Saturn. Under its ice is an ocean of salty water. Through cracks near its south pole, water sprays out into space like fountains. Living things need water, but also other ingredients. One of them is phosphorus, which living things use to build DNA, the instructions inside every cell. Did this hidden ocean have phosphorus?

Frank Postberg, a planet scientist at the Free University of Berlin in Germany, led the study. Scientists in Europe, Japan and the USA worked with him, including Christopher Glein of the Southwest Research Institute. They used old data from NASA's Cassini, a spacecraft that explored Saturn. They published in June 2023.

Cassini went round Saturn from 2004 to 2017. The icy spray from Enceladus feeds a faint ring of Saturn, called the E ring. Cassini flew through that ring many times. A tool on board, the Cosmic Dust Analyzer, caught tiny ice grains and worked out what each grain was made of. The team studied these old records again.

img.alt: A cutaway drawing of Enceladus showing a thick white ice shell, a blue ocean beneath it, and a rocky centre, with spray coming out at the bottom.

cards.b: Some ice grains held phosphates, which are phosphorus joined with other elements. Lab tests showed the ocean has at least 100 times more phosphate than Earth's oceans. It was the first time phosphorus was found in an ocean beyond Earth. Living things use phosphorus in DNA, in bones, and in the molecules that carry energy in cells.

img.alt: A drawing of the white, cracked moon Enceladus with a pale blue plume of spray rising from the bottom.

cards.b: The phosphate signal was clear in the ice grains, and lab tests backed it up. But having the ingredients is not the same as having life. Nobody has found life on Enceladus, or anywhere beyond Earth. Whether life could start in that ocean is still an open question.

Enceladus now seems to have water, salts, carbon-based chemicals and phosphorus. That makes it one of the best places to look for life in our solar system. The team's models also suggest that other icy moons with oceans could have lots of phosphate too. Future missions may go and sample the spray directly.

Cassini never touched the hidden ocean. It learned what was in it by studying the spray. Try a guessing game. Ask someone to secretly stir lemon juice into one cup of water, sugar into a second, and salt into a third. Dip a clean spoon in each and taste one drop. Can you tell what is hidden in each cup, without seeing it?

Imagine we found tiny living things in the ocean of Enceladus. Should we bring some back to Earth to study them closely? Or should we leave them alone in their own home, in case we harm them? What would you decide, and why?
